fixes.answer: In my view, the most important qualities are patience and [[consistency]]. Children thrive on stability, so a parent who sets clear, fair boundaries helps them feel secure. Equally vital is unconditional love balanced with the willingness to discipline when necessary. A good parent also [[leads by example]], since children tend to [[absorb]] behaviour far more than instructions.

Childhood has changed dramatically. In the past, children spent most of their free time playing outdoors and socialising in person. Today, much of that has been [[supplanted]] by screens, which I find rather [[disconcerting]]. Children are also under far more academic pressure now. So while modern children have more opportunities, they arguably have a less [[carefree]] upbringing.

I think childhood is profoundly [[formative]]. The experiences and relationships we have in those early years shape our personality, our self-esteem and how we relate to others. A secure, loving childhood tends to produce confident, well-adjusted adults, whereas a troubled one can leave lasting [[scars]]. In many ways, our childhood [[lays the foundation]] for everything that follows.
fixes.why: marked the full phrase 'lays the foundation'

fixes.answer: I expect parenting will become increasingly [[intertwined with]] technology. Parents will likely rely more on apps and online resources for guidance, and managing children's screen time will become an even more [[daunting]] challenge. I also anticipate a move towards more [[egalitarian]] parenting, with responsibilities shared more equally. Hopefully there will also be greater awareness of children's emotional wellbeing.
fixes.why: 'challenge' and 'emotional' are plain; used 'intertwined with' and 'daunting'

fixes.answer: The most effective way is by [[modelling]] those values themselves, since children imitate what they see. Beyond that, parents can use everyday situations as [[teaching moments]], discussing honesty or kindness openly. Encouraging empathy, perhaps through community involvement, also helps. Ultimately, values are [[instilled]] gradually through consistent example rather than through occasional lectures.

The clear advantage is financial; a [[dual income]] provides a higher [[standard of living]] and more opportunities for the children. It can also make both parents positive role models of independence. The downside is that it may leave less time for the children, potentially affecting the parent-child bond. It really [[comes down to]] the quality of the time spent, not just the quantity, and whether adequate childcare is in place.
fixes.why: 'bond', 'quantity', 'childcare' are plain; marked 'dual income', 'standard of living', 'comes down to'

fixes.answer: I partly agree. Modern parenting rightly encourages children's independence, but in some cases [[the pendulum has swung]] too far, and children lack clear boundaries. A total absence of limits can leave children feeling [[insecure]] rather than free. That said, the opposite extreme is equally harmful, so the goal should be freedom within a [[framework]] of sensible, loving guidance.
fixes.why: sir's line lists 'framework'; 'guidance' is plain; marked 'the pendulum has swung'
